title: Managing home electricity load when charging an EV
subtitle: Avoiding blown fuses and high bills by matching EV charge rate to available capacity
excerpt: An EV charger running at full speed can draw more power than the rest of a house combined. Managing the charge rate — through the charger settings, a load-management device, or a time-of-use tariff schedule — prevents tripping the main fuse and cuts the running cost by charging during cheap-rate hours.
sourceNotes: Ofgem EV smart charging guidance (2024); OZEV (Office for Zero Emission Vehicles) home charge grant guidance; BEAMA guidance on domestic EV charger installation.

glossaryTerms.definition: An Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment unit that delivers AC power to charge an electric car at home. Rated in kW — typically 3.7 kW (single-phase, 16 A) or 7.4 kW (single-phase, 32 A).
A system that monitors total household electrical load and automatically reduces EV charge rate when other high-draw appliances are running, to stay within the supply fuse rating.
An electricity tariff where the unit rate varies by time of day — typically cheaper overnight and dearer in the evening peak. Designed to reward flexible loads like EV charging.

content.text: draws 32 amps from a single-phase supply. Most UK homes are supplied at 60–100 amps. Running the charger alongside a cooker, a heat pump, and a dishwasher risks hitting the supply fuse rating.
prevents this by throttling the charge rate when other loads are high.

The supply fuse at your meter controls total maximum current. A 60-amp fuse allows a maximum of 13.8 kW continuous draw; an 80-amp fuse allows 18.4 kW. If your household draw peaks at 8 kW (heating, cooking, hot water all running), a 7.4 kW charger would take you to 15.4 kW — above the 60-amp limit. The fuse trips and the charger and possibly the house loses power.
The simplest approach: set the charger to start after 22:00 and finish before 06:00 when the household load is low. Most modern chargers have a built-in schedule. This also aligns with
off-peak hours — saving 12–18p/kWh against peak rate at 2025/26 prices.

Most smart chargers allow the maximum current to be set in the app — from 6 A (1.4 kW) up to 32 A (7.4 kW). Setting a permanent cap of 16 A (3.7 kW) halves the charge rate but also halves the instantaneous load. For a car used for typical commuting, a 3.7 kW charge rate overnight adds 40–50 km of range per hour — usually more than enough.
3. Install a dynamic load management CT clamp

A current transformer (CT) clamp fitted to the incoming supply cables at the consumer unit measures total household draw in real time. The charger reads this data and reduces its output automatically when household demand is high. This allows the EV to charge at full speed most of the time without the risk of overload — the charger throttles only when another large load starts.

Some chargers (Zappi, Wallbox Pulsar Plus, Myenergi Zappi) integrate with solar PV inverters to charge the car from solar surplus. The charger runs at the rate of surplus generation — 1.4 kW to 7.4 kW depending on how much sun is available. This is a more complex setup but makes good use of daytime generation that would otherwise be exported at low SEG rates.

rows.symptom: Supply fuse tripping at night when EV charger is running
rows.cause: Other loads (immersion heater timer, storage heater charge cycle) are also starting at the same time
rows.fix: Stagger the start times of each large load so they do not overlap. Use the charger's delay-start setting to begin charging 30–60 minutes after the immersion heater timer is scheduled.

rows.symptom: Charger throttles to 6A (1.4 kW) and never increases, even when no other loads are running
rows.cause: CT clamp wired in error or giving an inflated reading — the charger thinks demand is high when it is not
rows.fix: Check that the CT clamp is fitted to the incoming supply conductors, not to the charger's own circuit. A CT on the charger circuit creates a feedback loop.
